binders: Two neighboring finite-volume grid cells indexed i-1 and i with approximate cell averages Q_{i-1} and Q_i.
Their shared cell interface, represented in local coordinates as x = 0.
A Riemann solver and the numerical flux computed for that interface.
conclusions: Information from solving the interface Riemann problem is used to compute a numerical flux at the shared cell edge.
That numerical flux is used to update the cell averages over a time step.
An approximate Riemann solver may be used when an exact solution is computationally too expensive.
definitions_and_conventions: The left cell average Q_{i-1} supplies q_l and the right cell average Q_i supplies q_r; reversing them changes the local Riemann problem.
The numerical flux is an approximation to the correct physical flux through the shared interface.
The interface location x = 0 is a local-coordinate convention inherited from equation (1.11).
Riemann-solution information may consist of waves and speeds rather than only a pointwise state.
hypotheses: The interface Riemann problem uses the left state q_l = Q_{i-1} and the right state q_r = Q_i.
The available input data is the neighboring approximate cell averages.
implicit_context: The passage does not display a closed numerical-flux formula or a complete indexed update equation.
The Riemann solver can be exact or approximate; the essential input ordering and use in the flux/update remain the same.
The computed interface flux is part of a conservative finite-volume time step in the conservation-law setting.
No reconstruction beyond piecewise-constant cell averages is specified in this introductory description.

details: Adjacent cell averages become the ordered left and right states of a local Riemann problem.
The Riemann solution supplies information from which a numerical interface flux is computed.
The interface flux contributes to updating cell averages over the time step.
Approximate Riemann solvers are permitted when exact nonlinear solves are too costly.

undebatable_constraints: The left Riemann state is q_l = Q_{i-1} and the right state is q_r = Q_i.
Q_{i-1} and Q_i are approximate cell averages in neighboring cells.
The Riemann problem is solved at their shared interface to obtain information for a numerical flux.
The resulting numerical flux is used in a cell-average update over a time step.
The numerical flux must approximate the correct interface flux using the available cell-average data.
The source permits approximate Riemann solvers and does not require an exact nonlinear solution.
No particular numerical-flux functional, reconstruction, limiter, or time integrator is fixed by this passage.
